a.headline: Your AI starts every session already knowing your repo.
a.sub: Stacklit maps your codebase once and keeps the map fresh. Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and more read a few hundred tokens instead of crawling your files.

b.headline: Stop paying your AI to re-read your repo.
b.sub: Stacklit keeps a small, current map of your code. Your coding agent reads it first and goes straight to the right file.

c.headline: A map of your code your AI can actually use.
c.sub: Index your repo once. Stacklit keeps it fresh and gives your agent a few commands to find the right file.

cta.installHint: No install step. It writes the map and opens it.

worksWith.title: Works with the assistants you already use
worksWith.note: Setup covers 26 assistants. Any MCP client works through stacklit serve, and anything else can read stacklit.json.

problem.title: Agents start from zero every session.
problem.body: A coding agent does not remember your repo. Each session it opens files to find its way, and often opens the same ones again. One study of eight models found that 27 to 52 percent of their file views were repeats.
problem.caveat: Measured on SWE-bench Verified tasks that every model solved. It describes the habit, not Stacklit.

items.name: Index
items.text: Scan the repo and write the map. It runs locally, in tens of milliseconds on a small Go repo.

items.name: Connect
items.text: Wire the map into the tools you use. A git hook refreshes it after each commit.

items.name: Ask
items.text: The agent asks for the part of the map it needs, with a hard size limit.

items.name: The map
items.text: stacklit.json lists your modules, what each one exports and who depends on whom. You commit it next to your code. A few hundred tokens of it go to the agent at the start of a session.

items.name: The commands
items.text: query, slice, impact, path, hubs and explain. Each takes a token budget, so the answer is never bigger than you allow.

items.name: The hooks
items.text: A git hook refreshes the map after every commit. An optional Claude Code hook points a grepped name to where it is defined.

items.name: The MCP tools
items.text: stacklit serve gives any MCP client 15 tools, or 4 with the minimal profile.

proof.title: What we measured, including where grep wins
proof.intro: A benchmark, not an agent study. No model was involved. Each task asks where something is implemented, and we check whether the right file came back. Tokens are bytes divided by four.
proof.agentAbNote: Same tasks and model, with and without Stacklit.

items.name: MIT licensed
items.text: Read it, fork it, ship it.

items.name: Free
items.text: No paid tier and no account.

items.name: Runs locally
items.text: Your code stays on your machine.

items.name: No telemetry
items.text: The CLI makes no network calls.

items.q: Do I need an LLM key?
items.a: No. Stacklit parses your code with tree-sitter and uses no model. There is nothing to sign up for and no key to paste.

items.q: Does my code leave my machine?
items.a: No. The index is built locally and the CLI makes no network calls. Only the optional --summary flag sends anything, and only if you pass it. The HTML map can load small language logos from thesvg.org, and STACKLIT_MAP_ICONS=off turns that off.

items.q: What if the index is stale?
items.a: A git post-commit hook rebuilds it after each commit, and stacklit status tells you if it has drifted. You can also run stacklit generate in CI. The output has no timestamps, so the file only changes when the code does.

When you already know the exact name, and on small repos you can read whole. One grep is cheaper than loading a map. Stacklit helps with questions grep cannot answer in one step, like what depends on this module or where a new adapter belongs.

final.title: Try it on your repo.
final.text: It takes a minute, and you can delete one file to undo it.
